questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to try living in a place that wasn't european or north american. Singapore has a lot of similarities to the west, but is still a non-western country, which made it ideal for me.

I could also travel a lot during my studies (I only had mandatory classes on monday and tuesdays) and the reputation and quality of NUS is also very good.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Everything is easily accessible in English.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Had a few questions. Usually got an answer within a day - they are very effective!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Many different types of student accommodation. 

I lived at Pioneer House, which is pretty much the same as PGP: many different blocks of housing, where there is 7-8 dorm rooms per floor per block. You share bathroom/shower and kitchen with those 7-8 others.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
There is no meal plan at PGP/Pioneer House, but there is at some of the Halls or Resident Colleges if you prefer.

There is a very new and quite big kitchen which rarely gets used (I didn't cook once, since it cheaper and easier to just buy food from hawker centers, Fairprice og elsewhere).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
UTown > PGP and the different houses (incl. Pioneer) > Halls.

Halls are the oldest type of accomodation and therefore also not the best.
PGP/Pioneer House is on the opposite side of campus from UTown, but it's very close to the MRT station, which is very convenient to get into the city.
UTown feels kind of like a resort... In my opinion it's the best, but it's also highly sought after. You live 4 people in an apartment together there. I only applied for the A/C rooms at UTown, which I regret as getting a non-A/C room and then buying an A/C (not that expensive) is pretty much the same.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
My order of preference if I had to apply again would be:

1. UTown with A/C
2. UTown w/o A/C
3. Resident Colleges/PGP/Houses

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not too difficult and if you email them, they'll send the previous years syllabus so you can get it pre-approved.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You sign up for courses back home and when you get there you have I think 3 more rounds to secure courses, so don't sweat it if you don't get what you want when applying online.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: E-mail them. They're friendly, professional and helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I applied for (5 in total), but I dismissed one as I only wanted 4 courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't really have any... Have good grades, so the professor (who chooses which students are able to get his class) wants to have you in?

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some lecturers were pretty standard just like you would have back home. Others were from the best US and UK universities, which made classes quite interesting.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Game Theory was decently hard, but not more than I was expecting.

Urban Economics was relatively easy if you're comfortable with microeconomics (Mikro I og Mikro II on polit).

International Political Economy was relatively easy (there were no pre-requisites), so everyone can take this class, so if you know a bit about macro, such as exchange-rate stuff, then you'll be more than fine.

Public Finance was way harder than expected... It didn't have a lot of math but the conceptual stuff (drawing diagrams) and intuition got quite advanced, which made it a bit hard to track. The lectures contained a lot of material, which made it a bit hard to keep up if you didn't understand the last slide. -Name Redacted- our lecturer also likes to make the exams different from the tutorial questions, so you've to extrapolate what you've learned to different situations. The median score in the midterm was 13 out of 30 and you needed 15 to pass...

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lectures were similar. You prepare your tutorial questions from home and then present them in class (you don't get time to answer them in class). There is mandatory participation in tutorials, so you can't be travelling all the time unless you stack tutorials on the same days (I only had classes monday and tuesday).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 1. Game Theory & Applications to Economics (Micro III on polit), 2. Public Finance (Public Economics on polit), 3. Urban Economics (elective), 4. International Political Economy (political science course)

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Public Finance was interesting but clearly the hardest class I took
Game Theory can go as Micro III but the lecturers english is not the best, so sometimes hard to keep up with the math, when you don't really understand what is said

International Political Economy is very interesting and also quite easy if you don't want to overload yourself.

Urban Economics is also relatively easy: the tutorials are discussions moderated by the prof in groups of 10-12 people, where you discuss chapters in a book called "Triumph of the City", which I found as quite a fun way of teaching compared to standard economics teaching. Furthermore, there is a mandatory field trip: we went to Geylang, which is Singapores red light district, where an MP from the government (he is also a Social Entrepeneur from Geylang) showed us around and told stories of the migrant workers, sex workers and singaporeans who lived there. Really interesting and kind of like "Gadens Stemmer" in Denmark, where you get to see the "dark side" of Singapore and get to understand the daily life of migrant workers and also see a side of singapore, that suprisingly has a lot of drugs...

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I travelled a lot (as do many other exchange students): I was in Malaysia 3 times (Melaka, Kuala Lumpur, Penang), Lombok in Indonesia, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea. This costs quite a lot of money, so my personal spending would most likely be lower if I didn't travel as much, but almost all exchange students here utilize Singapore's very connected airport to travel ALL over asia.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food can be found pretty cheaply at hawker centers or food courts, but sometimes (in my opinion) the quality isn't the best, so I gravitated towards a bit more expensive places to eat, which made my spending on food go up quite a lot. If you like asian food, then Singapore is great: you can find cuisines from all over Asia here (even the world). If you have the money, there are also quite expensive restaurants that serve world class food.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I wanted to join the rowing club, but you'd to sign up for try-outs during the first month of the semester, which I missed because I was travelling.

So I ended up not being a part of any clubs other than the event my House hosted, which I kind of regret now - would have been nice to immerse myself a bit more into local life.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Volleyball, Football, Climbing, Food-related, Swimming, Rowing, Running, different crafts: there is a club for everyone I suppose, so if you're interested you'll probably find one that fits.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Idk I didn't really participate in many

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to Melaka in Malaysia if you're interested in the history of the Malacca Strait and colonial stuff.

Hong Kong was a top destination for me: kinda wish I'd gone there on exchange.

I climbed Mt. Rinjani on Lombok with some friends, which was a really fun hike (though also a bit strenous). 

Taiwan is soooo peaceful and beautiful: if you want a slower pace of life than in Singapore/HK, then go here.

Also remember to spend time exploring the different areas of Singapore: Fort Silosa for WW2 stuff, The National Gallery is good (had a monet exhibition), Sands Theatre had Les Miserables from West End which was really good, Marine Parade is a nice part of the city in my opinion and do the tourist stuff: Lau Pa Sat, Sentosa, MBS, Chinatown etc. Everyone travels so much that the country itself gets kind of neglected...

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
You don't clap after lectures - I don't make that mistake again...

Singapore is international so not too hard, but locals can be quite introverted (I guess in many ways similar to us scandinavians).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a club. I mostly made friends with other exchangers, which was nice, but I'd also have liked to have made more local friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Clapping after lectures is replaced by pure silence...

People reserve tables by leaving their umbrella/water bottle/tissues and then go order food.

It's very international and everything works efficiently in Singapore and is in English, so you'll be fine.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go here if you want: 1. The credentials of one of the best universities in the world, 2. The possibility to travel around SE asia like it was your gap year, 3. not having to pay extreme amounts of money in rent compared to north america

If you're more "creative" you'll probably find Singapore quite boring, as the local cultural scene is quite dead compared to other asian countries. Almost all students here want to work in finance/tech/business, so if that's ur thing then you'll fit right in. If you want a similar, but more exiciting city, then choose Hong Kong.

Oh, and prepare to be sweaty: it's very humid.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nope

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Travelling and trying new food

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Passing Public Finance and juggling travelling over the weekend with coming prepared to class

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
